items.stem: An AR(p) process is stationary if and only if:
options: all coefficients are less than 1 in modulus
every root lies inside the unit circle
every root of the AR polynomial lies outside the unit circle
items.explanation: Stationarity requires |B| > 1 for every root of φ(B) = 0. For an AR(1) the root is 1/φ, so the condition becomes |φ| < 1 — but option A fails in general, since (1.2, −0.4) is stationary with φ₁ > 1. Some texts state the condition for reciprocal roots, where it reads 'inside'.

items.stem: The stationarity condition for an AR(1) with coefficient φ is:
items.explanation: The root of 1 − φB = 0 is B = 1/φ, and |1/φ| > 1 is exactly |φ| < 1. Option A admits φ = −2, which is explosive; option D admits φ = 1, which is the random walk and non-stationary.
items.check: At φ = 1 the variance σ²/(1 − φ²) is undefined, so the inequality must be strict.

items.stem: The three conditions for an AR(2) to be stationary are:
items.explanation: All three are required, and together they describe a triangle with vertices (2, −1), (−2, −1) and (0, 1). Option A is insufficient: (0.6, 0.4) has both coefficients below 1 in modulus yet sums to exactly 1 and has a unit root.

items.stem: A finite-order MA process is:
options: stationary only if the coefficients sum to less than 1
items.explanation: yₜ = εₜ − θ₁εₜ₋₁ − ⋯ − θ_qεₜ₋q has mean 0 and finite constant variance σ²(1 + Σθᵢ²) for any coefficients, with autocovariances vanishing beyond lag q. So stationarity is automatic and only invertibility can fail.

items.stem: The invertibility condition for an MA(q) process concerns:
options: the roots of the AR polynomial
the roots of the MA polynomial
the sum of the coefficients only
items.explanation: Invertibility requires every root of θ(B) = 0 to lie outside the unit circle — the same condition as stationarity but applied to the MA polynomial instead of the AR one. That is why the two regions have the same shape.

items.stem: A pure AR process is:
items.explanation: Invertibility constrains the MA polynomial, and a pure AR process has none — equivalently θ(B) = 1, which has no roots. So the question of invertibility does not arise, and a pure AR question is always about stationarity.

items.stem: Is the AR(2) process with φ = (1.2, −0.4) stationary?
options: It cannot be determined from the coefficients
items.explanation: 0.8 < 1, −1.6 < 1 and |−0.4| < 1, so all three hold. The roots are a complex pair of modulus 1/√0.4 = 1.5811, comfortably outside the unit circle. None of the three conditions involves φ₁ alone, and the triangle extends to φ₁ = ±2.

items.stem: Is the AR(2) process with φ = (1.2, −0.2) stationary?
options: Yes, since 1.2 − 0.2 = 1.0 satisfies the first condition
No — it has a unit root
items.explanation: φ₁ + φ₂ = 1.0 exactly, which does NOT satisfy the strict inequality. The polynomial factors as (1 − B)(1 − 0.2B), so the roots are 1 and 5 and one sits on the unit circle — a unit root, so differencing is the repair. A numerical root-finder returns 1.0000000000000002 here, which is why boundary cases need algebra.

items.stem: The vertices of the AR(2) stationarity triangle are:
items.explanation: φ₁ + φ₂ = 1 meets φ₂ = −1 at (2, −1); φ₂ − φ₁ = 1 meets φ₂ = −1 at (−2, −1); and the two slanted edges meet at (0, 1). The base is at φ₂ = −1 and the apex at (0, 1).
items.check: The triangle must extend to φ₁ = ±2, since (1.2, −0.4) is stationary and so must lie inside it.

items.stem: An MA(2) with θ = (0.6, 0.4) under the convention yₜ = εₜ − θ₁εₜ₋₁ − θ₂εₜ₋₂ is:
items.explanation: Every finite MA is stationary. For invertibility the same three inequalities apply in θ, and θ₁ + θ₂ = 1.0 fails the first — the MA polynomial factors as (1 − B)(1 + 0.4B), with a root at 1. So it is stationary but not invertible.

items.stem: For a stationary AR(1) written as an infinite MA, the variance is:
items.explanation: yₜ = Σ(j≥0) φʲεₜ₋ⱼ, so the variance is σ²Σφ^(2j) = σ²/(1 − φ²), convergent exactly when |φ| < 1 — which is the stationarity condition. Summed numerically: 1.3333 at φ = 0.5, 2.7778 at 0.8 and 10.2564 at 0.95.
items.check: The variance must exceed σ², since the series starts with the term j = 0 and all terms are positive.

items.stem: Consider stationarity and invertibility conditions.
items.explanation: A is true, as (1.2, −0.4) shows. B is true — a finite MA has finite constant variance for any coefficients. C is true: the same three inequalities apply in θ under the minus convention. D is false — the two constrain different polynomials and are entirely independent.
statements: An AR(2) can be stationary with φ₁ > 1.
A finite-order MA process is stationary for any coefficient values.
The MA(2) invertibility region is the same triangle as the AR(2) stationarity region.
A process that is stationary must also be invertible.

A.why: True. (1.2, −0.4) satisfies all three conditions, with complex roots of modulus 1.5811. The triangle extends to φ₁ = ±2.

B.why: True. The variance σ²(1 + Σθᵢ²) is finite and constant whatever the coefficients, and the autocovariances vanish beyond lag q, so stationarity is automatic.

C.why: True, under the minus convention: θ₁+θ₂ < 1, θ₂−θ₁ < 1, |θ₂| < 1. Both are the condition that a polynomial's roots lie outside the unit circle.

D.why: False. The conditions constrain different polynomials and are independent, which is why all four combinations occur — for instance φ = 0.5 with θ = 1.3 is stationary but not invertible.

items.stem: For an AR(2) with complex roots, the modulus of each root is:
items.explanation: The product of the two roots of 1 − φ₁B − φ₂B² is −1/φ₂, and for a conjugate pair that product is the squared modulus, so |B| = 1/√|φ₂|. The stationarity condition then reduces to |φ₂| < 1 alone in the complex case.
items.check: At (1.2, −0.4) the discriminant 1.44 − 1.6 is negative so the roots are complex, and 1/√0.4 = 1.5811 matches the computed modulus.

items.stem: An MA(1) with θ = 2 and one with θ = 0.5 have:
items.explanation: ρ₁ = −θ/(1 + θ²) is unchanged by replacing θ with 1/θ: both give −0.4, and all higher autocorrelations are zero. So the two are observationally identical, which is precisely why the invertibility restriction |θ| < 1 exists — to select one representative and make the parameter identified. Simulation at both values gave −0.3996.

items.stem: An ARMA(1,1) with φ = 0.3 and θ = 1.5 is:
items.explanation: Two independent checks: |0.3| < 1 so the AR side is stationary, while |1.5| > 1 so the MA side is not invertible. The equivalent invertible coefficient is 1/1.5 = 0.667, which gives the same autocorrelations and is what should be reported.

items.stem: Why does invertibility matter in practice, beyond being a convention?
options: it removes the need for differencing
it guarantees the variance is finite
it lets εₜ be written in terms of the observed past, which forecasting requires
items.explanation: For a chosen MA parameterisation, invertibility makes its inverse filter converge so the innovations can be recovered from observed values. A non-invertible parameterisation has an observationally equivalent invertible representation after rescaling the innovation variance; forecasts from the observed process use that canonical form. Finite variance is delivered by stationarity, which a finite MA has automatically.

items.stem: Consider the derivation and use of the AR(2) triangle.
items.explanation: A is true — the first two conditions are φ(1) > 0 and φ(−1) > 0. B is true: with complex roots the modulus is 1/√|φ₂|. C is true, and it is why algebra beats a root-finder on boundaries. D is false — the edge φ₁ + φ₂ = 1 is the SINGLE unit root edge; the double unit root sits at the vertex (2, −1).
statements: The conditions φ₁ + φ₂ < 1 and φ₂ − φ₁ < 1 are φ(1) > 0 and φ(−1) > 0.
When the discriminant φ₁² + 4φ₂ is negative the root modulus is 1/√|φ₂|.
A numerical root-finder can wrongly pass an exact unit root as satisfying |B| > 1.
The edge φ₁ + φ₂ = 1 corresponds to a double unit root.

A.why: True. φ(1) = 1 − φ₁ − φ₂ > 0 rearranges to φ₁ + φ₂ < 1, and φ(−1) = 1 + φ₁ − φ₂ > 0 to φ₂ − φ₁ < 1. They say the polynomial does not vanish at B = ±1.

B.why: True. The product of the roots is −1/φ₂, which for a conjugate pair equals the squared modulus. At (1.2, −0.4) that gives 1/√0.4 = 1.5811.

C.why: True, and it happened during this lesson's verification: for (1.2, −0.2) the roots came back as 1.0000000000000002 and 4.999999999999999, so a test of |B| > 1 passed. Factorising as (1 − B)(1 − 0.2B) settles it.

D.why: False. That edge has ONE root equal to 1 — for (1.2, −0.2) the roots are 1 and 5. The double unit root is at the vertex (2, −1), where both roots approach 1 and two differencings are needed.

items.stem: Σ(j≥0) φ^(2j) for φ = 0.95 equals approximately:
items.explanation: The sum is 1/(1 − φ²) = 1/(1 − 0.9025) = 1/0.0975 = 10.2564, which is the variance of a stationary AR(1) with σ² = 1 and φ = 0.95. Summed numerically over 2,000 terms as 10.256410.
items.check: As φ approaches 1 the variance diverges, so a value near 1 must give a large number — which rules out options B and D at once.

items.stem: A maximum-likelihood routine returns an MA coefficient of exactly 1.000 with a very large standard error. The best reading is:
options: the optimiser has failed and should be restarted
the estimate is on the invertibility boundary, where the likelihood flattens — often from over-differencing
the series needs a second differencing
items.explanation: θ = 1 is the edge of the invertible region, and a standard error comes from the curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum — nearly zero on a flat boundary. The commonest cause is over-differencing, which manufactures an MA(1) with θ exactly 1 and ρ₁ = −0.5, so the first thing to check is whether the differencing was necessary rather than adding terms.

items.stem: Two analysts fit the same series and report θ = 0.5 and θ = 2.0, with identical fitted values. The best description is:
options: the two models differ in their autocorrelations but not their fitted values
one analyst has made an arithmetic error
the models are observationally identical, and only θ = 0.5 is invertible, so that is the one to report
items.explanation: The autocorrelation function is invariant under θ ↦ 1/θ. The full autocovariance structure also matches when the innovation variance is rescaled: for θ* = 1/θ, take σ*² = θ²σ². The two are observationally equivalent parameterisations; |θ| < 1 selects the canonical representation in which the shocks are recoverable from the observed past.
